before.exam_tip_html: Truth table questions award one mark per correct output cell — not one mark for the whole table. Always write every row, include intermediate columns for combined circuits, and never leave a cell blank. For a two-input truth table, you need exactly four rows. For XOR specifically, double-check the (1,1) row: the output is 0, not 1, because the inputs are the same. In describe or explain questions about logic gates, name the operator (AND/OR/NOT/XOR/NAND/NOR) and state the condition that produces a 1 output.
before.content_html:
What Are Logical Operators?

Computers make decisions by evaluating conditions that are either true or false. Logical operators are the building blocks of this decision-making. They combine Boolean values — values that are either 1 (true) or 0 (false) — and produce a Boolean result. In hardware, these operators are implemented as logic gates. In software, they appear inside if statements and while loops. Understanding them is essential for both circuit design and programming.

A truth table is the standard way to describe a logical operator’s behaviour. Each row represents one combination of inputs. For two inputs A and B there are four possible combinations: (0,0), (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1). You must always show every row — leaving rows out drops marks in the exam.

Key Fact

There are four logical operators you need to know: AND, OR, NOT and XOR. Each has a standard symbol used in circuit diagrams and a truth table showing every possible input-output combination.

The AND Operator

AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1. Think of it as a strict gatekeeper: every condition must be met. In Boolean notation, AND is written with a dot or by placing letters side by side: A·B or AB.

ABA AND B
000
010
100
111

The OR Operator

OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1. It only outputs 0 when both inputs are 0. In Boolean notation, OR is written with a plus sign: A + B.

ABA OR B
000
011
101
111

The NOT Operator

NOT is a single-input operator that inverts its input: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0. It is also called a complement or inverter. In Boolean notation, NOT is written as an overbar — for example, NOT A is written as Ā (A with an overbar) — or sometimes as A′ or !A.

ANOT A
01
10

The XOR Operator

XOR (exclusive OR) outputs 1 when the inputs are different. If both inputs are the same — both 0 or both 1 — the output is 0. XOR is denoted A ⊕ B. It is particularly useful in binary addition circuits (half adders) and encryption.

ABA XOR B
000
011
101
110
Key Fact

XOR outputs 1 only when its two inputs differ. This distinguishes it from OR: OR outputs 1 when both inputs are 1, but XOR outputs 0 in that case because the inputs are the same.

Real circuits chain several gates together. Consider the expression NOT A AND B. To build the truth table, add an intermediate column for NOT A before the final output column.

ABNOT ANOT A AND B
0010
0111
1000
1100

Notice the extra intermediate column. In the exam, when a question includes a combined circuit, fill in every intermediate column — each cell can earn an independent mark. Do not skip straight to the output column.

The most common error in truth table questions is confusing XOR with OR. Remember: OR outputs 1 for the row (1,1), but XOR outputs 0 for that row because the inputs are the same. Write the row (1,1) carefully for every XOR column.

A second mistake is filling in only the output column for combined-gate questions. The mark scheme awards one mark per correct cell, including intermediate columns. If the question shows a two-stage gate circuit, add an intermediate column for each gate stage and fill every row before moving to the final output.

A third mistake is mixing up Boolean notation with arithmetic. In Boolean expressions, A·B means AND and A + B means OR. The + symbol does NOT mean addition here. Students who confuse arithmetic addition with Boolean OR often get three-variable expressions wrong.

NAND and NOR Gates

Two additional gates appear in this course: NAND and NOR. A NAND gate is AND followed by NOT — its output is the inverse of AND. A NOR gate is OR followed by NOT — its output is the inverse of OR. NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any logic circuit can be built from NAND gates alone (or NOR gates alone).

ABNANDNOR
0011
0110
1010
1100

Notice that NAND outputs 0 only in the last row (both inputs 1), while NOR outputs 1 only in the first row (both inputs 0). These are exactly opposite to AND and OR respectively. The practical importance of universal gates is that hardware manufacturers can produce one type of gate in bulk and use it to build every other gate, simplifying chip design and reducing manufacturing costs.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1; NOT inverts its single input; XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ.
  • For combined-gate truth tables, add an intermediate column for each gate stage and fill every cell — each cell earns an independent mark.
  • NAND and NOR are the inverse of AND and OR respectively, and are called universal gates because any circuit can be built from either one alone.

before.exam_tip_html: In a “simplify a Boolean expression” question, write the law name beside every step. The 2024 examiners’ report flagged Boolean simplification as a weak area, with students stopping at a partial simplification and missing the Absorption or Complement law that finishes the job. After each step, scan the expression: does A + A·B appear? (Use Absorption.) Does A + A̅ appear? (Use Complement.) Always check whether your answer can be simplified further before writing your final result.

practice_questions.text:
Which Boolean algebra law states that A + A = A?
A) Identity
B) Complement
C) Idempotent
D) Annulment
State De Morgan's first law in words.
practice_questions.marks: NOT(A AND B) equals NOT A OR NOT B [1 mark]. Accept equivalent overbar notation.

practice_questions.text: Simplify the Boolean expression A·1 + A·NOT(A), showing the law used at each step.
practice_questions.marks: Step 1: Identity law — A·1 = A; expression becomes A + A·NOT(A) [1]. Step 2: Complement law — A·NOT(A) = 0; expression becomes A + 0 [1]. Step 3: Identity law (OR form) — A + 0 = A [1]. Final answer: A [1]. Award each mark for the correct application of the named law.

practice_questions.text: Simplify the Boolean expression NOT(A OR B) OR A, showing the law applied at each stage.
practice_questions.marks: Step 1: De Morgan's second law — NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B; expression becomes NOT(A)·NOT(B) + A [1]. Step 2: Distributive law — factor (NOT(A) + A)·(NOT(B) + A) or apply Complement to NOT(A) + A = 1 [1]. Step 3: Complement on A + NOT(A) = 1 [1]. Result: NOT(B) + A (via Commutative) or equivalent simplified form [1]. Accept any correct step-by-step route to the correct simplified form.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Absorption law A + A·B = A is true. You may use a truth table to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: When A = 0: 0 + 0·B = 0 = A for any B [1]. When A = 1: 1 + 1·B = 1 = A for any B [1]. Therefore the B term adds nothing to the result — whenever A is 0 the whole expression is 0, and whenever A is 1 the whole expression is 1 [1]. The expression reduces to A alone [1].

practice_questions.text: A student claims that A·B + A·NOT(B) = A. Show, using Boolean algebra laws, whether this claim is correct.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Step 1 applies Distributive law to factor out A: A·(B + NOT(B)) [law named]; Step 2 applies Complement: B + NOT(B) = 1 [law named]; Step 3 applies Identity: A·1 = A [law named]; conclusion that the claim is correct with all three laws correctly named and applied.
Secure: Correct simplification to A with at least two laws correctly named; minor labelling error in one step.
Developing: Correct simplification shown but fewer than two laws named; or one step skipped.
Emerging: Some attempt to factor the expression; does not reach correct conclusion.

before.content_html:
What Is an Operating System?

Every computer needs software that manages its hardware and gives applications a platform to run on. An operating system (OS) sits between the hardware and the user-facing applications. Without an OS, every application would have to contain its own code for drawing text on screen, reading keyboard input and writing to disk — an enormous duplication of effort. The OS handles these common tasks so that applications can focus on their specific job.

The core of the OS is the kernel. The kernel runs continuously in the background, managing resources and mediating between hardware and software. It is the most privileged piece of software on the system — it can access all hardware directly, while applications must go through the kernel via system calls.

Key Fact

An operating system manages six key areas: CPU scheduling, memory management, backing store (file system) management, peripheral management, the user interface, and security. Each area has dedicated OS components.

CPU Management and Scheduling

A modern computer runs many processes at the same time — a web browser, a music player, background updates. The OS scheduler decides which process gets CPU time and for how long. Because the CPU switches between processes so rapidly, it creates the illusion of true simultaneous execution even on a single-core processor.

Two common scheduling algorithms are:

  • Round-robin scheduling: each process gets a fixed slice of CPU time (a quantum) in turn. When a process’s quantum expires, the next process in the queue takes over, even if the first process hasn’t finished. This ensures fairness — no single process can monopolise the CPU.
  • First-Come-First-Served (FCFS): processes run in the order they arrive in the queue. Simple to implement but unfair — a long process arriving first can block shorter ones for a long time.

Interrupts allow the OS to respond to urgent events without waiting for the current process to finish. When a key is pressed or a network packet arrives, the hardware sends an interrupt signal. The CPU pauses its current task, saves its state, handles the interrupt, then resumes what it was doing. Without interrupts, a computer could not respond to user input while running a program.

Memory Management

The OS controls how RAM is allocated between running programs. When more programs are open than RAM can hold, the OS uses paging — dividing memory into fixed-size blocks called pages. Inactive pages are moved to a reserved area of the hard drive called the backing store (virtual memory). When those pages are needed again, they are swapped back into RAM.

Virtual memory allows a computer to run programs that collectively need more RAM than is physically installed. The trade-off is speed: swapping pages to and from secondary storage is much slower than RAM access. If too much paging occurs, the system slows dramatically in a state called “thrashing.”

Key Fact

Paging divides RAM into fixed-size pages. Inactive pages are written to the backing store (virtual memory) on secondary storage. Accessing the backing store is slower than RAM, so excessive paging causes the system to slow down.

Peripheral and File System Management

Peripherals — printers, keyboards, mice, external drives — each speak a different communication protocol. The OS uses device drivers: small software modules that translate between the OS’s generic commands and the specific signals each device understands. When you plug in a USB keyboard, the OS loads the relevant driver so that keystrokes reach the running application correctly.

The OS also manages the file system — how files are organised, named, stored and retrieved on backing storage. It maintains a directory structure (folders and subfolders), controls which users can read or write which files, and handles the physical reading and writing of data to the storage medium. Common file systems include NTFS (Windows), ext4 (Linux) and APFS (macOS).

User Interface and Security

The OS provides a user interface — the layer through which people interact with the computer. The two main types are the graphical user interface (GUI, which uses windows, icons and a pointer) and the command-line interface (CLI, which accepts typed commands). The OS also enforces security: user account authentication (logins and passwords), access permissions on files and folders, and software privilege levels that prevent applications from accessing each other’s memory.

Utility software is system software that maintains and optimises the computer. Unlike applications (which do user tasks like word processing), utilities work on the system itself. You need to know the following utilities and what each one does:

  • Anti-virus software: scans files and processes for known malicious patterns (virus signatures) and removes or quarantines threats. Relies on regular signature updates.
  • Backup software: makes copies of files to a separate location (external drive, cloud). Full backups copy everything; incremental backups copy only files changed since the last backup.
  • Disk defragmenter: on traditional hard drives, files become fragmented — stored in non-contiguous sectors. A defragmenter reorganises files into contiguous blocks, reducing read-head movement and improving access speed. (Not needed on SSDs.)
  • Disk compression: reduces the size of files on disk by encoding data more efficiently. Saves storage space at the cost of small processing overhead when reading and writing.
  • Data recovery software: attempts to retrieve files that have been accidentally deleted or corrupted. Works because “deleting” a file usually only removes the directory entry — the data often remains until overwritten.
  • File manager: provides a graphical or command-line interface to browse, copy, move, rename and delete files and folders. Windows Explorer and Finder are examples.

Beyond the six main utilities above, the specification also references:

  • Archiver / compression utility: packages multiple files into a single compressed archive (e.g. ZIP, RAR). Useful for sending groups of files and reducing download sizes.
  • Partition editor: divides a physical storage device into separate logical sections (partitions), each of which can hold a different file system or operating system.
  • Clipboard manager: extends the standard cut-and-paste clipboard to store a history of copied items, allowing users to paste earlier copied content.
  • System profiler / diagnostic tool: reports detailed information about hardware (CPU type, RAM installed, GPU) and software (driver versions, installed applications). Used to diagnose compatibility and performance issues.
  • Cryptographic utility: encrypts or decrypts files and communications using cryptographic algorithms, protecting sensitive data from unauthorised access.
  • Revision control (version control): tracks changes to files over time, allowing earlier versions to be restored. Essential in software development (e.g. Git). Useful even for individual documents.

Students sometimes confuse the categories of software. The key distinction is purpose: the OS manages hardware resources and provides a platform; application software performs end-user tasks (word processing, gaming, browsing); utility software maintains the system. A word processor is not a utility; anti-virus software is not the OS. All three are software, but they serve distinct functions.

A second common confusion: utility software is part of system software (alongside the OS), but utility software is not the same as the OS. The OS kernel runs at the lowest level and starts first; utilities are higher-level tools that run on top of the OS and can be installed or removed independently.

glossary_terms.definition: Software that manages computer hardware and software resources, providing common services for application programs and acting as an interface between the user and the hardware.
The central component of an operating system that manages the CPU, memory, device drivers and system calls, and runs with the highest level of hardware privilege.
The OS process that decides which program or process uses the CPU next and for how long, enabling apparent multi-tasking on a single processor.
A signal sent to the CPU by hardware or software to indicate that an event requires immediate attention, causing the CPU to pause its current task.
An area of secondary storage used by the OS to temporarily store memory pages that do not currently fit in RAM, extending the apparent size of main memory.
Software designed to help manage, maintain and optimise a computer's hardware and operating system, rather than to perform end-user tasks.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The OS manages CPU scheduling (round-robin or FCFS), memory (paging and virtual memory via backing store), peripherals (via device drivers), the file system, the user interface, and security.
  • Interrupts let the CPU respond to urgent hardware or software events without waiting for the current process to finish.
  • Utility software maintains the system: key examples include anti-virus, backup, disk defragmenter, disk compression, data recovery, file manager, archiver, partition editor, clipboard manager, system profiler, cryptographic utility and revision control.
before.exam_tip_html: In “describe” questions about the OS, name the specific function and explain what it does — “the OS manages memory” scores zero; “the OS uses paging to divide RAM into fixed-size blocks and swaps inactive pages to the backing store when RAM is full” scores full marks. For utility software questions, give the utility’s name and a sentence on what it does and why. Compare questions often ask you to contrast two utilities or an OS function with a utility — always state what each one does before comparing. In discussion questions about impacts of technology, the 2024 examiners’ report noted that balanced answers (one-sided responses score lower) are needed.
